title: Verb Tenses
subtitle: Chrono's Tower of Time
intro: Chrono the time wizard guards a tower with twelve rooms, one for each English tense. Climb it floor by floor: past, present and future, each in simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous forms.

rules.title: Simple Present
rules.tagline: Habits, facts and things that are always true

story.line: Welcome to the ground floor of my tower, the Room of Always.
Why is it called that?
Because here we speak of habits and facts. The sun rises in the east. Kaito eats ramen every day.
True. I eat ramen every day.
Notice: I eat, you eat, but he eats. With he, she or it, the verb grows an -s. That is the one trick of this room.

parts.name: Form
parts.detail: Base verb. Add -s or -es for he/she/it.
parts.example: I walk, she walks, it goes

parts.name: Negative
parts.detail: do not / does not + base verb.
parts.example: He doesn't like spiders.

parts.name: Question
parts.detail: Do / Does + subject + base verb?
parts.example: Does she train on Sundays?

parts.name: Uses
parts.detail: Habits, facts, schedules, and feelings.
parts.example: The train leaves at 8. Water boils at 100°C.

rules.history:
Old English verbs had different endings for every person: ic singe, þū singest, hē singeþ (I sing, thou singest, he singeth). Over time almost all of them wore away.

The only survivor is the third-person -s. It spread from the dialects of northern England, and by about 1600 it had beaten the southern -eth ending. That's why he walks has an -s while I walk doesn't. It's a fossil!

examples.good: She speaks three languages.
He doesn't eat meat.
examples.note: After does, use the base verb with no -s.

examples.good: Cats sleep a lot.

rules.trick: He, she, it: the S is lit! (he runs, she sings, it works)

rules.title: Present Continuous
rules.tagline: Happening right now: am / is / are + -ing

story.line: On the second floor, everything is in motion. Clocks spin. Water flows upward.
This is the Room of Right Now. What are you doing, Hana?
I am climbing your tower!
Am climbing. A form of be, plus a verb wearing -ing. The action is in progress, like a movie paused mid-scene.
And I'm planning a prank for later. Hehe.
Yes, this room can also show future plans that are already arranged.

parts.name: Form
parts.detail: am / is / are + verb-ing.
parts.example: They are training.

parts.name: Now
parts.detail: An action happening at this moment.
parts.example: Look! It's snowing.

parts.name: Temporary
parts.detail: A situation that isn't permanent.
parts.example: I'm staying with my aunt this week.

parts.name: Planned future
parts.detail: Arranged plans.
parts.example: We're leaving tomorrow.

parts.name: Stative verbs
parts.detail: Verbs of state (know, like, want, believe) don't usually take -ing.
parts.example: I know the answer. (not I'm knowing)

rules.history:
Forms like 'he is reading' existed in Old English but were rare. The continuous really took off between about 1500 and 1800.

Even the passive version 'the house is being built' is fairly young. It first appeared in the late 1700s, and some grammarians attacked it as ugly. Before that, people said 'the house is building' to mean the same thing.

examples.good: I am reading a manga.
She is studying abroad this year.
I want some tea.

rules.trick: If you could film it happening right now, use be + -ing.

quiz.why: Know is a stative verb, so use simple present.

rules.title: Simple Past

story.line: Look through this window. It shows the past.
That's me yesterday! I walked to the shrine and I trained.
Walked, trained. Regular verbs add -ed to travel into the past.
And I goed to the ramen shop!
Ah, go is a rebel. It becomes went. We will meet the rebels on the next floor.
And questions and negatives use did: Did you go? I didn't go. After did, the verb returns to its base form.

parts.name: Regular form
parts.detail: Add -ed (or -d if the verb ends in e).
parts.example: jump → jumped, love → loved

parts.name: Spelling changes
parts.detail: Consonant + y → -ied; short vowel + consonant → double it.
parts.example: study → studied, stop → stopped

parts.name: Negative & questions
parts.detail: did / didn't + base verb.
parts.example: Did you see it? I didn't see it.

parts.name: Use
parts.detail: Finished actions at a known past time.
parts.example: We met in 2020.

rules.history:
The -ed ending comes from a very old Germanic ending -da or -ta, which some scholars believe was once a form of the verb 'do.' If that's right, 'I walked' started out as something like 'I walk-did.'

This -ed method is called the 'weak' past tense. It became the default for new verbs, which is why modern words like texted, googled and emailed all use it.

examples.good: She studied all night.
Did you finish your homework?
examples.note: After did, use the base verb.

examples.good: The bus stopped suddenly.

rules.trick: Did is a time machine for the whole sentence. Once did goes to the past, the verb can stay home in its base form.

quiz.why: Short vowel + consonant: double the n.
After didn't, use the base verb.

rules.title: Irregular Verbs

story.line: The third floor is a battlefield. Rebel verbs refuse to wear -ed.
I teached them a lesson! I catched them all!
Taught. Caught. You're a walking grammar mistake.
These rebels are among the oldest words in English. Instead of adding -ed, they change their vowel: sing, sang, sung. Drink, drank, drunk.
So I just have to memorize them?
Yes, but most belong to families that follow patterns. Learn the families and the battle gets easier.

parts.name: Three forms
parts.detail: Base, past, past participle.
parts.example: write – wrote – written

parts.name: Vowel-change family
parts.detail: sing-sang-sung, ring-rang-rung, swim-swam-swum.
parts.example: She swam across the river.

parts.name: -ought / -aught family
parts.detail: buy-bought, think-thought, teach-taught, catch-caught.
parts.example: I bought a new sword.

parts.name: No-change family
parts.detail: cut, put, hit, set, let, cost.
parts.example: Yesterday I cut my hair.

parts.name: Total rebels
parts.detail: go-went-gone, be-was/were-been.
parts.example: He went home.

rules.history:
Irregular verbs are what linguists call 'strong verbs.' They come from Proto-Germanic, spoken over 2,000 years ago, where changing the vowel (called ablaut) was the normal way to make a past tense.

Old English had hundreds of strong verbs. Over the centuries many switched to -ed: 'help' once had the past 'healp' and 'holpen.' The ones that survive are the verbs people use most often, because frequent words are remembered and resist change. Went is a special thief: it was stolen from the old verb 'wend' (to go).

examples.good: I have written three letters.
examples.note: After have, use the past participle.

examples.good: She brought snacks.
The vase broke.

rules.trick: Learn them in rhyming families, like a theme song: sing-sang-sung, ring-rang-rung, drink-drank-drunk.

quiz.why: After have, use the past participle: seen.

rules.title: Past Continuous
rules.tagline: In progress in the past: was / were + -ing

story.line: On this floor, the past is frozen mid-motion.
Look, it's last night! I was sleeping when the alarm rang.
Was sleeping is the long background action. Rang is the short event that interrupted it.
And I was eating ramen while Yumi was stealing my egg!
Two long actions at the same time. Use while for that.

parts.name: Form
parts.detail: was / were + verb-ing.
parts.example: They were laughing.

parts.name: Interrupted action
parts.detail: Long action (past continuous) + short action (simple past).
parts.example: I was cooking when the phone rang.

parts.name: Parallel actions
parts.detail: Two things in progress at once, often with while.
parts.example: While she was reading, he was painting.

parts.name: Scene setting
parts.detail: Describes the background of a story.
parts.example: The wind was howling and the lanterns were flickering.

rules.history:
Like the present continuous, this form grew popular in Early Modern English (1500s to 1700s). Writers loved it for storytelling, because it lets them paint a background scene and then drop an event into it.

This 'background + event' pattern is so useful that storytellers today still begin with it: 'It was raining when the stranger arrived.'

examples.good: We were walking home when it started to rain.
examples.bad: We walked home when it was starting to rain.
examples.note: The long action is walking; the interruption is started.

examples.good: While Hana was studying, Kaito was sleeping.
They were watching anime at 9 p.m.
examples.bad: They was watching anime at 9 p.m.

rules.trick: Long action = was/were + -ing (the background music). Short action = simple past (the sound effect).

quiz.why: The shower was the long action interrupted by the call.

rules.title: Present Perfect
rules.tagline: Past actions connected to now: have / has + past participle

story.line: This floor is a bridge. One end touches the past, the other touches now.
I have visited Kyoto three times!
Perfect. We don't care exactly when. We care that it's part of your life up to now.
I have visited Kyoto yesterday!
No! Yesterday is a finished time. Once you name a finished time, cross back to simple past: I visited Kyoto yesterday.

parts.name: Form
parts.detail: have / has + past participle.
parts.example: She has finished.

parts.name: Life experience
parts.detail: At some time up to now; the exact time doesn't matter.
parts.example: I have seen that movie.

parts.name: Unfinished time
parts.detail: Started in the past and still true, with for or since.
parts.example: I have lived here for five years.

parts.name: Recent news
parts.detail: With just, already, yet.
parts.example: He has just left.

parts.name: Never with finished time
parts.detail: Not with yesterday, last week, in 2019.
parts.example: I saw it last week. (not I have seen it last week)

rules.history:
The present perfect started as a possession phrase. In Old English, 'ic hæbbe þone fisc gefangenne' meant roughly 'I have the fish (in a) caught (state).' You literally possessed the result.

Over time 'have' lost its meaning of owning and became a helper verb, and the word order shifted to 'I have caught the fish.' It's a sentence that slowly turned into a tense.

examples.good: I have never eaten sushi.
She has worked here since 2020.
examples.note: Since + a starting point needs the present perfect.

examples.good: I lost my keys yesterday.
examples.bad: I have lost my keys yesterday.

rules.trick: Present perfect is a bridge. If you can see a finished time word (yesterday, ago, last year), the bridge collapses: use simple past.

options: She has called me an hour ago.
She called me an hour ago.
She has call me an hour ago.
She calling me an hour ago.
quiz.why: An hour ago is a finished time.

rules.title: Past Perfect
rules.tagline: The past before the past: had + past participle

story.line: Hana reaches a room with two windows into the past, one behind the other.
When I arrived at the station, the train had left.
Two past events. Which came first?
The train left first, then I arrived. So the earlier one gets had.
Exactly. Had + past participle is the deeper past. It's how storytellers do flashbacks.

parts.name: Form
parts.detail: had + past participle (same for every subject).
parts.example: They had eaten.

parts.name: Earlier past
parts.detail: The action that happened before another past action.
parts.example: She had finished when I came.

parts.name: With by, already, before
parts.detail: Common partners.
parts.example: By noon, we had climbed the mountain.

parts.name: Third conditional
parts.detail: Appears in 'if' regrets.
parts.example: If I had known, I would have helped.

rules.history:
The past perfect developed alongside the present perfect, from 'had' plus a participle. Old English already used it, and translators of Latin found it handy for the Latin pluperfect tense, whose name means 'more than perfect.'

In everyday speech today, people often skip it when words like before or after already make the order clear: 'I ate before I left' is fine.

examples.good: When we got there, the movie had started.
examples.bad: When we got there, the movie started.
examples.note: Without had, it sounds like it started at the moment we arrived.

examples.good: She had never seen snow before that trip.
examples.note: Experience up to a past moment.

examples.good: By the time Kaito woke up, Yumi had eaten his breakfast.

rules.trick: Had = 'had already happened.' It's the flashback inside your flashback.

quiz.q: 'I couldn't get in because I ___ my keys.'
quiz.why: Losing the keys happened before not getting in.
Duration up to a past moment: had been.

rules.title: Will vs. Going To

story.line: The top floors show the future. But English has no single future tense. It borrows helpers.
I will become the strongest swordsman!
Will: a promise, a decision made right now, or a prediction.
I'm going to visit my grandmother next week. I already bought the ticket.
Going to: a plan you already made, or a prediction with evidence. Look at those clouds. It's going to rain!

parts.name: will + base verb
parts.detail: Quick decisions, promises, offers, general predictions.
parts.example: I'll help you. It will be fine.

parts.name: be going to + base verb
parts.detail: Plans made before now; predictions based on what you can see.
parts.example: Watch out! You're going to fall.

parts.name: Present continuous
parts.detail: Fixed arrangements with a time and place.
parts.example: I'm meeting Yumi at six.

parts.name: Simple present
parts.detail: Timetables and schedules.
parts.example: The festival starts on Friday.

rules.history:
Old English had no future tense at all. People used the present tense and context.

Will comes from Old English willan, 'to want.' Shall comes from sculan, 'to owe or be obliged.' Over centuries these words lost their meanings of wanting and owing and became future helpers. 'Going to' joined in the late 1400s, when 'I am going (on a journey) to do something' turned into a way of describing plans.

examples.good: The phone is ringing. I'll get it!
examples.bad: The phone is ringing. I'm going to get it!
examples.note: A decision made right now → will.

examples.good: We're going to move to Osaka in May.
Look at that wave! It's going to crash!

rules.trick: Will = a sudden spark. Going to = a plan already in your pocket.

quiz.q: 'It's cold in here.' 'OK, I ___ close the window.'
quiz.why: A decision made at that moment.

rules.title: Future Continuous & Future Perfect
rules.tagline: will be doing / will have done

story.line: Final floors. Let's look into the future.
At 8 p.m. tomorrow, I will be performing at the festival!
Will be + -ing: an action in progress at a future moment. The future continuous.
By the end of the year, I will have defeated 100 opponents!
Will have + past participle: something finished before a future deadline. The future perfect. Words like by are its best friends.

parts.name: Future continuous
parts.detail: will be + verb-ing. In progress at a future time.
parts.example: This time next week, I'll be lying on a beach.

parts.name: Future perfect
parts.detail: will have + past participle. Finished before a future time.
parts.example: By 2030, she will have graduated.

parts.name: Signal words
parts.detail: this time tomorrow (continuous); by, by the time (perfect).
parts.example: By the time you arrive, we'll have eaten.

rules.history:
These tenses are built like Lego from pieces English already had: will (future) + be + -ing (continuous) or will + have + participle (perfect).

That's why English can express time so precisely without inventing new endings. Latin needed special verb endings for its future perfect; English just stacks helper verbs.

examples.good: Don't call at 9. I'll be sleeping.
By Friday, I'll have finished the project.
examples.bad: By Friday, I'll finish the project.

examples.good: She will have worked here for ten years next month.
examples.note: Duration up to a future point.

rules.trick: See 'by + future time'? Reach for will have + done.

quiz.q: 'At noon tomorrow we ___ over the ocean.'

rules.title: Perfect Continuous Tenses
rules.tagline: How long something has been going on

story.line: Kaito stumbles in, drenched in sweat.
What happened to you?
I have been training for six hours!
Have been + -ing. It focuses on the duration, and often on visible results, like that sweat.
Move it into the past: he had been training for six hours when he collapsed. Or the future: by midnight, he will have been training for ten hours.
And I have been laughing at him for six hours.

parts.name: Present perfect continuous
parts.detail: have / has been + -ing. Started in the past, still going or just stopped.
parts.example: It has been raining all day.

parts.name: Past perfect continuous
parts.detail: had been + -ing. Duration before a past moment.
parts.example: She had been waiting for an hour when the bus came.

parts.name: Future perfect continuous
parts.detail: will have been + -ing. Duration up to a future moment.
parts.example: In May, I'll have been studying English for a year.

parts.name: Signal words
parts.detail: for, since, all day, how long.
parts.example: How long have you been learning?

rules.history:
These are the youngest and longest English tenses, combining the perfect (have + participle) with the continuous (be + -ing). They became common in the 1700s and 1800s as the continuous spread throughout the language.

With these, English can say four-word verb phrases like 'will have been studying,' which would surprise an Old English speaker who had just two simple tenses: present and past.

examples.good: I've been waiting for 20 minutes!
Her eyes were red. She had been crying.
examples.note: A past result with a cause before it.

examples.good: How long have you been living here?
examples.bad: How long are you living here?
examples.note: Ask about duration with have been.

rules.trick: When the question is 'how long?', the answer usually wears been + -ing.

quiz.q: 'We ___ for two hours. Let's take a break.'
'He was tired because he ___ all night.'
